chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, and others, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the believing man who marries a Christian and a Jew, he (the Imam) said: If he consummates the marriage with the Muslim woman, what does he do with the Jewess and the Christianess? I said to him: He will have desire for them. He said: If he does, he must prevent them from drinking wine and eating pork. And know that there is a slight displeasure (ghadadhah) upon him regarding their religion. And what has occurred in the manner of these narrations which included the permissibility of marrying Jewish and Christian women, they bear aspects of interpretation: one being that they may have been expressed as taqiyya (dissimulation), because all those who differ from us go to the permissibility of that, so it is permissible that these narrations came in agreement with them, just as their counterparts came for that reason. And another being that these narrations may have referred to the permissibility of marrying the weak-minded (or simple) women among them, who do not hold disbelief with firm adherence to it and tribal loyalty to it. And for one with this description, the marriage contract is permissible. This indicates it.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a Muslim man marrying a Christian or Jewish woman according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi records Imam al-Sadiq’s nuanced ruling that while a Muslim man may marry a Kitabi woman, he bears the religious burden of preventing her consumption of wine and pork, reflecting a practical guardianship. The Imam further contextualizes the apparent permissibility in other narrations as either *taqiyya* (dissimulation) to align with opposing schools or as specific to *Musta'dafat* (weaker-minded) women who are not firmly entrenched in disbelief, highlighting the Shia emphasis on theological stability in interfaith marriage.
